description: When a habit feels too big to start, shrink it to two minutes; small starts have a way of growing on their own.

body.heading: Starting is the steepest part
paragraphs: Most resistance lives in the first moments. A thirty-minute practice session sounds heavy at 7 a.m.; two minutes of it sounds like nothing. That difference is not laziness — it is the honest shape of motivation, which usually arrives after we begin, not before.
The two-minute version is a doorway, not a cheat. You walk through it by doing the tiniest real version of the habit: open the document, put on the shoes, play one scale, read one paragraph.

body.heading: Give yourself full permission to stop
paragraphs: The rule only works if stopping after two minutes is genuinely allowed. Some days you will stop, and that is fine: you still showed up, and showing up is the habit you are actually building.
On many days, though, you will find yourself continuing. Motion creates its own momentum, and the task that felt enormous from the sofa often feels ordinary once your hands are in it.

body.heading: Grow it slowly, if at all
paragraphs: After a few weeks of easy starts, the two minutes may stretch naturally. Let it. Resist the urge to immediately raise the target just because things are going well; a habit that stays pleasant is a habit that stays.
And on the hardest days, come back to the doorway. Two minutes is always there, and it is always enough to keep the thread unbroken.

takeaway: Shrink the start to two minutes, and let momentum decide the rest.
